And when I'm talking about information, I'm talking about state security information which was part and parcel of the job he did.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have to note that Jovica Stanisic, from the moment the commission was set up and it started working and in the course of its work and even when the commission issued its report, still held his office and he was never moved or suspended from that office, from that position. He came to work from time to time, he had the same powers that he always had, but his room for manoeuvre was somehow limited, and his powers were limited. According -- on the order of the chief of service, certain information and intelligence was given to him and not to Jovica Stanisic as the assistant chief for that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I've had a note passed to me saying a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then we'll take a break. We have been informed by Mr. Bakrac that he has no questions if nothing will be triggered by the Prosecution. Ms. Marcus, how much time would you need?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the moment I'll have to stick by my original estimate, which was between two to two and a half hours. I would say two sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, I do not know how much more time you need at this moment. We come close to the point where we are in dangerous waters, that is, running out of time, unless you say, No, those two sessions are fully available for Ms. Marcus tomorrow or even later today, part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I would hope to finish almost all of it today, with maybe just a slight slip-over until tomorrow, maybe of 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But then we are -- I mean, that is hardly any time for the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'll finish today, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll finish today. And we'll then immediately take a break in order to -- we are -- we resume at ten minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, you asked for -- to address the Court. If it would be because you are seeking an extension of time for responding to the 92 bis motion of DST-071, please tell me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: It's also, Your Honour, because I wanted to seek leave to make an oral response with respect to DST-070 and DST-072. Those are also 92 bis witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. An extension of time for 71?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: One week after the filing of a corrigendum, which the Defence asserts would be by the 13th of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, any objection against an extension of time for the response to DST-071?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac? You're wisely -- yes, yes, Mr. Bakrac, I wondered whether you would --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That request is granted. You have one week on from the filing of the corrigendum. Oral submissions, how much time would you need?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Maybe ten minutes or so. Maybe a little bit more. I mean, with your leave, I can make the submission tomorrow. But today is the dead-line. But if the Chamber so orders, of course, I can make that submission tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We give an extension of time of one day to Ms. Marcus so that we first try to conclude the evidence of this witness. I would, at this point in time, Ms. Marcus, I would really prefer that. Yes, extension of time of one day is granted, and we'll see further tomorrow whether it needs two days.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And my apologies for perhaps putting a lot of pressure on these matters. Could the witness please be escorted into the courtroom. Ms. Marcus, again, without the pressure, I would have given you an hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Understood, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Lekovic, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Would you please have a look at D00283, and the 65 ter number is 1D04874. This is -- looks as though it's a letter which went to various services requesting that they as part of this investigation also conduct their own investigations; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This document is not to be shown to the public, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if it has already been shown, we need a redaction. It has not yet been shown. Please proceed. If you ask specific questions about it, should we move into private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, although I think we can avoid mentioning names, I hope. Names of individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if the document in itself is under seal, I don't have a clear recollection of what reasons it exactly was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Neither do I, so perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps out of an abundance of caution we move into private session, and what you've said until now seems not to be of a kind to require a redaction. But it's your exhibit, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think that Your Honour is right. I don't think so far any redaction is required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave it in your hands as matters stand now, and we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Lekovic, you -- I want to return to the issue of depoliticization of the service. How did Stanisic go about that process?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Firstly, SPS cells were not set up within the state service either in the organisational units either -- or in the administration for Belgrade or in the headquarters of the service. Secondly, even if somebody was in favour of the SPS, or even a member of the SPS or some other party, they were not supposed to demonstrate that openly at work. And thirdly, the same criteria were to be applied in the work, irrespective of what political party was being investigated or which official thereof.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: When you speak of SPS cells, what are you describing?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness sit closer to the microphone or could the microphone be brought closer to the witness. The interpreters have a problem hearing him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Every political party has its platform, has its bodies, elected bodies, as well as local organisations at lower levels. The method of the party's work is regulated by the statute of the party. These would be local cells or boards of the SPS in local communes, in companies, and institutions. There were people who were civil servants, but they were not allowed to display their party loyalty at work. They could only do that at their place of residence. They could set up their boards and assist board meetings at their place of residence. They were not supposed to openly display their loyalty or affiliation to a political party at work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I did not see any action taken upon the request of the interpreters to have the microphone be closer to the witness. I don't know whether this was ... I now see that action is taken.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you want me to repeat my answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I don't think there's any need for that, but there was request for you to come closer to the microphone or the microphone come closer to you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] It was done, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Lekovic, when you speak of Mr. Stanisic fighting to depoliticize the State Security Service, which period are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm referring to a period towards the end of 1990. On the 17 of July, 1990, there was the founding congress of the SPS. And then in September there were last meetings of the League of Communists. It was then said that the party organisations of the League of Communists were being disbanded, that people could go to local party offices to get hold of their documents, and from then on there would be the SPS instead of the League of Communists. This was the watershed moment when the wheels were put in motion in order to depoliticize the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could you say the year again when you say Mr. Stanisic was fighting to depoliticize the party -- the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We are talking about the three or four last months of 1990. And then in the upcoming period when things had to be proven to the general public, and to the citizens to show that the service was finally depoliticized, that people who were in the service were not politically engaged in any of the political parties, and also that the State Security Service put a ban on setting up a local party board.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know what Mr. Stanisic's position was when he took over as chief of the state security in relation to these issues?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, what issues?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Depoliticization of the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did not have a political role to play.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what about his position in relation to politics within the DB?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What position do you have in mind? I find your question a bit odd. His position was for the service to do its work, to be a professional service and to only do those things for which it was originally set up and for which it existed. Nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were there any SPS units or cells within the DB after Stanisic took over as chief?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were no cells or boards or units or branches of the SPS.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, two quick subjects or quick issues in relation to your Official Note. Could you turn, please, to page 6 of the English and page 6 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that not to be shown --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Not to the shown to the public, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not to be shown to the public. Do we need to move into private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's probably best, Your Honour, yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Lekovic, we would like to see you back tomorrow morning, the 12th of October, at 9.00 in the morning, and then we'll further hear your testimony through a videolink from this Courtroom II. We stand adjourned.
